```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(RADAR)
```

# Overview and installation

RADAR (**R**aman spectral **A**nalysis using **D**eep learning for **A**rtifact
**R**emoval) separates spectra into baseline, cosmic rays, noise and Raman
peaks. This standalone R package provides inference, automatic differentiation,
Adam training, synthetic spectra, evaluation, spectral file handling and maps.
Both pretrained architectures and their weights are included as native R
objects. Installation and model loading require no downloads or conversion.

R 4.1.0 or later is required. Core computation uses base and recommended R
packages. Optional packages support particular file formats, as listed below.
Install a source archive using:

```{r installation, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("RADAR_0.1.0.tar.gz", repos=NULL, type="source")
library(RADAR)
vignette("RADAR", package="RADAR")
```

To build documentation from source, install knitr, rmarkdown and Pandoc.
Run `R CMD build RADAR`, then `R CMD check --no-manual RADAR_0.1.0.tar.gz`.
The distributed archive includes a rendered guide.

# Quick start

```{r quick-start}
sample_data <- generate(2, length=128, seed=7)
parts <- RADAR::decompose(sample_data$X, model="standard")
names(as.list(parts))
plot(parts, index=1)
```

Rows of a matrix are spectra and columns are spectral points. A vector is one
spectrum. The last dimension of a map array is spectral. R indices start at one.
Use `RADAR::decompose()` and `RADAR::write()` to avoid conflicts with similarly
named functions in other packages. `$peaks` holds corrected Raman bands.
Input intensities are normalized per spectrum; output uses input intensity
units by default. Inspect decompositions before downstream interpretation.

# Reading spectra and choosing a file format

`RADAR::read()` chooses a reader from the extension. `read_spectra()` is an
alias. Set `format` when an extension is missing, ambiguous or misleading.
`RADAR::write()` similarly chooses an output format; it accepts spectral
records, plain numeric arrays, decompositions and synthetic datasets. Explicit
namespacing distinguishes these functions from base R's `read` and `write`.

```{r files-working-data}
files_dir <- tempfile("radar-vignette-files-")
dir.create(files_dir)
files_axis <- seq(400, 1800, length.out = 64)
files_peak <- exp(-0.5 * ((files_axis - 1000) / 65)^2)
files_X <- rbind(
  40 + 0.015 * files_axis + 180 * files_peak,
  55 + 0.010 * files_axis + 130 * files_peak,
  35 + 0.020 * files_axis + 210 * files_peak,
  60 + 0.008 * files_axis + 160 * files_peak
)
files_positions <- as.matrix(expand.grid(y = 0:1, x = 0:1)[, c("x", "y")])
files_data <- spectral_data(
  files_X, wavenumbers = files_axis,
  names = c("top_left", "bottom_left", "top_right", "bottom_right"),
  positions = files_positions, position_names = c("x", "y"),
  map_shape = c(2, 2), x_units = "cm-1", y_units = "counts",
  meta = list(instrument = "vignette example")
)
files_csv <- file.path(files_dir, "spectra.csv")
RADAR::write(files_data, files_csv)
files_back <- RADAR::read(files_csv)
print(files_back)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(files_back$intensities, files_X,
                          check.attributes = FALSE)))
```

The example uses temporary, deliberately short spectra to keep the vignette
quick to run. It demonstrates the interface rather than a measured-spectra
accuracy benchmark.

## Format capabilities and optional packages

The package's current registry is available programmatically:

```{r files-format-registry}
files_formats <- formats()
files_formats[, c("format", "extensions", "read", "write", "requires")]
```

| Format | Extensions | Read / write | R requirements and scope |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Delimited text | `.csv`, `.tsv`, `.tab`, `.txt`, `.dat`, `.asc`, `.prn`, `.xy` | Both | Base R; wide, row and long tables; comma, semicolon, tab, pipe or whitespace input; decimal commas and instrument text exports. |
| RRUFF | `.rruff`; also RRUFF text saved as `.txt` | Read only for `.rruff` | Base R; `##` preambles/trailers and numeric spectral pairs. |
| R spectral records | `.rds` | Both | Base R; preserves the native record and metadata. A spectral RDS file is distinct from a saved model RDS file. |
| JSON | `.json` | Both | `jsonlite`; RADAR records, simple `x`/`y` arrays or lists of named spectrum objects. |
| NumPy array | `.npy` | Both | Native R parser/writer; one rectangular array, without a spectral axis or other record metadata. |
| NumPy archive | `.npz` | Both | Native R array parser plus `jsonlite` for RADAR metadata; archives use R's zip/unzip facilities and a system zip utility for writing. |
| Thermo Galactic GRAMS SPC | `.spc` | Both | Native R; old `0x4D` and new `0x4B`/big-endian `0x4C` input, single and multiple spectra, common or per-spectrum axes, integer or IEEE float intensities. Writes new-format float data. |
| JCAMP-DX | `.jdx`, `.dx`, `.jcamp`, `.jcm` | Both | Native R; 4.24/5.x, AFFN and ASDF SQZ/DIF/DUP compression, XYDATA, XYPOINTS/PEAK TABLE pairs, scale factors and compound LINK blocks. |
| HDF5 / NetCDF-4 | `.h5`, `.hdf5`, `.he5`, `.nc`, `.nc4` | Both | `hdf5r`; `jsonlite` for RADAR metadata. Reads numeric HDF5 datasets, including spectral maps; this is not a classic NetCDF reader. |
| SQLite | `.db`, `.sqlite`, `.sqlite3` | Both | `DBI`, `RSQLite`, and `jsonlite` for RADAR metadata. Table selection or SQL queries; RADAR output uses `spectra` and `radar_metadata` tables. |
| Excel | `.xlsx`, `.xlsm`, `.xls` | Read; write `.xlsx` | `readxl` for input; `openxlsx` and `jsonlite` for output. Select sheets by name or one-based index, or use `sheet = "all"`. |
| Parquet | `.parquet`, `.pq` | Both | `arrow`; `jsonlite` for RADAR metadata. Long tables by default. |
| Feather / Arrow | `.feather`, `.arrow` | Both | `arrow`; `jsonlite` for RADAR metadata. |
| MATLAB | `.mat` | Both | Native numeric level-5 parser, including compressed elements and numeric arrays inside structs/cells; `jsonlite` for RADAR metadata and output. HDF5-backed v7.3 also requires `hdf5r`. |
| Renishaw WiRE | `.wdf` | Read only | Native R binary reader for spectra, axes and scan positions. |
| Horiba LabSpec 6 | `.xml` | Read only | `xml2`; native handling of the LabSpec LSX spectral rows and calibrated axes. |
| Princeton Instruments TriVista | `.tvf` | Read only | `xml2`; ordinary frames and axes in the first document. |

Install only the optional R packages required by the formats you use. The
network itself, plotting, RDS, delimited text, SPC and JCAMP-DX do not require
these optional packages. A missing adapter dependency produces an R package
installation message when that format is used.

Several boundaries matter when exchanging files:

* JCAMP-DX NTUPLES data are unsupported.
* MATLAB level 4, complex spectra and export of unequal-length spectra are
  unsupported. Use HDF5, NPZ, JSON or RDS for ragged spectra. HDF5-backed
  MATLAB reading concerns numeric datasets; arbitrary MATLAB objects are not
  reconstructed.
* NumPy object/pickle arrays are unsupported. Integers are represented as R
  doubles; exact values above `2^53` are not guaranteed.
* SPC output uses 32-bit IEEE intensities, so round-trip differences from R
  doubles are expected. NPY holds no axis, names, coordinates or metadata.
* `.xls` is read only; export to `.xlsx`. Vendor formats are read only.
  TriVista split glued child datasets are unsupported.
* WITec `.wip` projects, Bruker OPUS binaries, Thermo OMNIC `.spa`, Andor `.sif`
  and Princeton `.spe` camera files are not read directly. Export them from
  the instrument software as SPC, JCAMP-DX, MATLAB or a text table.

## Wide, row and long tables

Text, Excel, Parquet, Feather and SQLite share the same table interpretation.
`layout = "auto"` is convenient when the file follows a familiar layout.
An explicit layout removes ambiguity in an unfamiliar export.

| Layout | Spectra arrangement | Axis and coordinate convention |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `"wide"` or `"columns"` | One spectrum per column | A monotonic first numeric column is the spectral axis. A labelled axis column also disambiguates short spectra. |
| `"rows"` | One spectrum per row | A monotonic first numeric row or numeric header supplies the axis. Leading empty cells in the axis row reserve columns for scan coordinates. |
| `"long"` | One spectral point per row | Columns such as `spectrum`, `name`, `x`, `y`, `z`, `wavenumber`, `intensity`; component columns can hold a decomposition. |

Column matching ignores case and spaces. Common spectral-axis names include
`wavenumber`, `raman shift`, `shift`, `wavelength`, `#wave`, `x-axis`,
`frequency`, `cm-1`, `pixel` and `channel`. Intensity aliases include
`intensity`, `counts`, `#intensity`, `signal`, `y`, `absorbance` and `cps`.
Scan coordinates can be labelled `x`, `y`, `z`, `#x`, `#y`, `time` or `depth`.
A repeated axis, a spectrum identifier or coordinate columns separate long
records into spectra. Different axes or lengths remain separate rather than
being silently interpolated onto a shared grid.

```{r files-table-layouts}
files_wide <- file.path(files_dir, "wide.csv")
RADAR::write(files_X, files_wide, wavenumbers = files_axis,
             names = files_data$names, layout = "wide")
files_wide_back <- RADAR::read(files_wide, layout = "wide")

# A row-oriented export: the first row is the axis.
files_rows <- file.path(files_dir, "rows.tsv")
utils::write.table(rbind(files_axis, files_X), files_rows, sep = "\t",
                   row.names = FALSE, col.names = FALSE, quote = FALSE)
files_rows_back <- RADAR::read(files_rows, layout = "rows")

# The map written above is a tidy table, including spectrum and coordinates.
head(utils::read.csv(files_csv, check.names = FALSE), 3)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(files_rows_back$intensities, files_X,
                          check.attributes = FALSE)))
```

## Instrument text dialects and text options

| Export | Reader behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| Renishaw WiRE text | Recognises `wl int`, `x wl int`, `y x wl int`, repeated spectral axes, and headers such as `#X #Y #Wave #Intensity`; retains scan positions. |
| Horiba LabSpec text | Skips `#key=value` instrument headers; recognises an axis row beginning with empty coordinate cells, followed by `x y i1 i2 ...` rows. |
| Ocean Insight / OceanView text | Reads the block between `>>>>>Begin Spectral Data<<<<<` and the end marker. |
| RRUFF text | Skips `##` descriptive header and end lines. |
| WITec, Wasatch Enlighten, B&W Tek and similar exports | Uses the generic two-column or table rules. Recognition of a text export does not imply support for that vendor's proprietary project files. |
| European numeric exports | Detects semicolon/tab separation and decimal commas such as `1234,5`; `decimal = ","` can force the decimal mark. |

Text options are `layout`, `delimiter`, `decimal`, `comments`, `skip_header`
and `encoding`. `comments = "#"` is the default; recognised instrument column
headers beginning with `#` are retained. `skip_header` discards a specified
number of initial lines. `encoding` specifies a text encoding when the
instrument's encoding needs to be supplied explicitly. Input field separators
can be comma, semicolon, tab, pipe or whitespace. The writer's delimiter
follows its format: comma for CSV and tab for TSV/text.

```{r files-decimal-text}
files_eu <- file.path(files_dir, "decimal-comma.csv")
writeLines(c("Instrument export", "Raman shift;Intensity",
             "100,5;1,25", "101,5;2,25", "102,5;3,25"), files_eu)
files_eu_back <- RADAR::read(files_eu, delimiter = ";", decimal = ",",
                            skip_header = 1)
files_eu_back$wavenumbers
files_eu_back$intensities

# Use a tab-separated output when retaining a decimal comma.
RADAR::write(files_data, file.path(files_dir, "decimal-comma.tsv"),
             decimal = ",", layout = "long")
```

A record without a conventional extension can still be read explicitly:

```{r files-format-override}
files_unknown <- file.path(files_dir, "measurement.export")
file.copy(files_wide, files_unknown)
files_explicit <- RADAR::read(files_unknown, format = "csv", layout = "wide")
```

## Spectral records, selection and maps

`spectral_data()` and its alias `SpectralData()` construct the same S3 record
returned by `read()`. A numeric vector is one spectrum, a matrix has spectra
in rows, and an array has the spectral dimension last. Native R map arrays
use dimensions `c(ny, nx, length)` and R's column-major ordering. A list can
hold spectra of unequal lengths.

| Record field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `$intensities`, `$spectra` | Aliases for the primary spectra: an `n` by `length` matrix, or a list for ragged data. |
| `$arrays` | All named spectral arrays in the file; for example `intensity`, or `spectra` and the four components. |
| `$wavenumbers` | Shared spectral axis, one axis per ragged spectrum, or `NULL`. |
| `$names` | Spectrum names, or `NULL`. |
| `$positions`, `$position_names` | One coordinate row per spectrum and labels for the coordinate columns. |
| `$map_shape` | Regular grid dimensions, or `NULL`; read from the file or inferred from a complete coordinate grid. |
| `$x_units`, `$y_units` | Spectral-axis and intensity units. |
| `$meta`, `$metadata` | Metadata aliases, including available instrument/file information. |
| `$source` | Source file path, when the record came from a file. |

A spectral record is a list. Unlike a decomposition, its ordinary
`length()` and `[` operate on list fields. Count or select its spectra through
the intensity matrix, and build another record if the selected spectra need
their axis and names attached:

```{r files-record-selection}
nrow(files_data$intensities)       # number of spectra
ncol(files_data$intensities)       # points per spectrum
is.list(files_data$intensities)    # ragged data use a list
files_selected <- spectral_data(
  files_data$intensities[c(1, 3), , drop = FALSE],
  wavenumbers = files_data$wavenumbers,
  names = files_data$names[c(1, 3)],
  positions = files_data$positions[c(1, 3), , drop = FALSE],
  position_names = files_data$position_names,
  x_units = files_data$x_units
)
dim(as_map(files_data, "spectra"))
```

For ragged records use `length(data$intensities)` and
`lengths(data$intensities)`. `as_map(data, "spectra")` reshapes a regular
record; use `load_components()` to obtain a decomposition with map access to
all its components. Explicit physical x/y coordinates determine grid
placement where available. File matrix row order remains unchanged.
Metadata records the C/F map order needed when importing files without
physical coordinates from row-major files.

## Container keys, Excel sheets and SQLite queries

In a foreign HDF5, NPZ, MATLAB or JSON container, an explicit `key` selects the
spectral array. Without it, the reader looks for familiar array and axis names
and otherwise uses numeric-array heuristics, including array size and likely
orientation. Supply `key` if that choice is ambiguous. A matching numeric
axis is kept; multidimensional spectral maps are flattened into spectrum
rows while retaining grid dimensions. The
`Regions/<region>/Dataset` HDF5 layout is also recognised and its regions are
combined into a matrix.

```{r files-container-keys}
if (requireNamespace("hdf5r", quietly = TRUE) &&
    requireNamespace("jsonlite", quietly = TRUE)) {
  files_h5 <- file.path(files_dir, "spectra.h5")
  RADAR::write(files_data, files_h5)
  files_h5_back <- RADAR::read(files_h5, key = "intensity")
  stopifnot(identical(dim(files_h5_back$intensities), dim(files_X)))
}
```

The following examples require your own files and are therefore shown without
being run:

```{r files-foreign-containers, eval=FALSE}
measurement <- RADAR::read("measurement.h5", key = "experiment/spectra")
measurement <- RADAR::read("measurement.npz", key = "spectra")
measurement <- RADAR::read("measurement.mat", key = "measurement/spectra")
measurement <- RADAR::read("measurement.json", key = "intensity")
measurement <- RADAR::read("workbook.xlsx", sheet = 2)       # R indexing starts at 1
measurement <- RADAR::read("workbook.xlsx", sheet = "run_A")
all_sheets <- RADAR::read("workbook.xlsx", sheet = "all")
names(all_sheets$arrays)
```

Excel defaults to the first data sheet, except that a RADAR decomposition
workbook with all five recognised component sheets is read together.
`sheet = "all"` reads all data sheets into named arrays; the
`radar_metadata` sheet is treated as metadata. When the sheets contain
unrelated measurements with different axes, read them separately.

SQLite defaults to the `spectra` table when it exists. `table` chooses
another table; `query` supplies a SQL query returning spectral table columns.
Keep the axis/value columns and the spectrum identifier or coordinates when
selecting a long-table subset.

```{r files-sql-selection}
if (all(vapply(c("DBI", "RSQLite", "jsonlite"), requireNamespace,
               logical(1), quietly = TRUE))) {
  files_db <- file.path(files_dir, "spectra.db")
  RADAR::write(files_data, files_db)
  files_one <- RADAR::read(
    files_db,
    query = "SELECT * FROM spectra WHERE spectrum = 2 ORDER BY wavenumber"
  )
  stopifnot(nrow(files_one$intensities) == 1)
  files_one$names
}
```

A SQL subset does not necessarily remain a complete map. Inspect its
coordinates and dimensions before reshaping it as a grid.

# Decomposing vectors, matrices, maps and files

| Argument | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `spectra` | Required | In-memory spectra, a spectral record or a file path. |
| `model` | `"ensemble"` | Bundled `"ensemble"`/`"standard"`, a saved model file or a loaded `radar_model`. |
| `wavenumbers` | `NULL` | Axis attached to the result; inherited from a spectral record when omitted. The network does not use the axis values. |
| `normalize` | `TRUE` | Min-max scale each spectrum before prediction. |
| `units` | `"original"` | Return input intensity units; `"normalized"` keeps network-scale components. |
| `batch_size` | `32` | Prediction grouping parameter; native R evaluates each spectrum separately to bound attention-layer memory. |
| `output` | `NULL` | Also write the result to a file. |
| `verbose` | `0` | Positive values print spectrum progress. |
| `...` | None | Reader options when `spectra` is a path: `layout`, `key`, `sheet`, `query`, etc. |

The executable example reuses one loaded model. The standard model's noise
head is the residual, so its components reconstruct the input. The ensemble
predicts noise independently and usually has a nonzero reconstruction
residual. Inspect a few examples with either model before applying it to a
large collection.

```{r decompose-main}
files_model <- load_model("standard")
files_components <- RADAR::decompose(files_data, model = files_model)
files_components
max(abs(files_components$residual))
```

All the following calls use the same interface. They are shown without
running extra predictions in this vignette:

```{r decompose-input-forms, eval=FALSE}
one <- RADAR::decompose(files_X[1, ], model = files_model,
                        wavenumbers = files_axis)
many <- RADAR::decompose(files_X, model = files_model,
                         wavenumbers = files_axis)
cube <- array(files_X, dim = c(2, 2, ncol(files_X)))
map <- RADAR::decompose(cube, model = files_model, wavenumbers = files_axis)
from_file <- RADAR::decompose(files_csv, model = files_model, layout = "long")
written <- RADAR::decompose(files_csv, model = "ensemble",
                            output = file.path(files_dir, "components.rds"))
```

A vector produces vector component fields. A matrix or map produces matrices
with one row per spectrum; map shape is kept separately. A list of
**equal-length** vectors becomes a matrix. A list of **different-length**
vectors, or a ragged SPC/JCAMP record, returns a list containing one
`radar_components` object per spectrum. Supply an axis list for ragged data:

```{r decompose-ragged, eval=FALSE}
ragged_spectra <- list(files_X[1, ], files_X[2, 1:48])
ragged_axes <- list(files_axis, files_axis[1:48])
ragged_parts <- RADAR::decompose(ragged_spectra, model = files_model,
                                wavenumbers = ragged_axes)
for (i in seq_along(ragged_parts)) {
  save_components(ragged_parts[[i]],
                  file.path(files_dir, paste0("ragged_", i, ".rds")))
}
```

The ragged branch does not accept a single `output` path: save each returned
object separately. Unlike a rectangular record, the separate ragged results
do not automatically carry all the parent record's per-spectrum names and
coordinates; preserve those separately if they are needed.

## Scaling and intensity units

For each spectrum, with offset `a = min(x)` and range `s = max(x) - min(x)`,
normalization is `(x - a) / s`. Flat spectra use `s = 1`, avoiding division
by zero. On return to original units, all components are multiplied by `s`
and `a` is added **only to the baseline**. This preserves the standard model's
additive relationship. Apart from numerical precision, changing an input's
affine intensity scale changes the output components by the corresponding
scale and baseline offset. A very large cosmic ray can compress the rest of
the normalized spectrum into a small interval.

```{r decompose-scaling}
files_scaling <- minmax_normalize(files_X)
range(files_scaling$normalized[1, ])
files_scaling$scaling$offset
files_components$meta$offset
files_components$meta$scale
```

```{r decompose-normalized, eval=FALSE}
normalized_parts <- RADAR::decompose(files_X, model = files_model,
                                     units = "normalized")
already_scaled <- RADAR::decompose(files_scaling$normalized,
                                   model = files_model, normalize = FALSE)
raw_predictions <- predict(files_model, files_scaling$normalized)
```

The axis is descriptive metadata: no automatic resampling, sorting or
interpolation occurs during decomposition. A descending axis and its
intensities stay in file order. Missing or infinite intensities are rejected;
clean, interpolate or crop them first. Point spacing matters scientifically
because the learned peak widths are expressed in sample points.

# Inspecting, selecting and plotting the results

A decomposition is an S3 `radar_components` list. Access its input,
estimates, axis and metadata with `$`; `Components()` is the constructor
alias for building an object from existing arrays.

| Field | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `$spectra` / `$original` | Input on the selected intensity scale. |
| `$baseline`, `$cosmic_rays`, `$noise`, `$peaks` | The four estimated components, with matching shapes. |
| `$wavenumbers`, `$names`, `$positions`, `$position_names`, `$map_shape`, `$x_units` | Available axis, identity and scan information. |
| `$units`, `$model` | Intensity scale and model architecture. |
| `$meta` / `$metadata` | Offsets, scales, normalization flag and available source metadata. |
| `$n_spectra`, `$length` | Spectrum count and channel count; `length(result)` also returns the spectrum count. |

Source file metadata are retained under
`result$meta$source_metadata`. Use `unclass(result)` when an ordinary list of
its stored fields is useful. The derived fields below are calculated when
accessed and need not be stored as additional arrays.

| Derived field | Definition | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `$corrected` | `peaks` | Clean Raman signal for subsequent analysis. |
| `$denoised` | `spectra - noise` | Remove noise while retaining baseline and cosmic rays. |
| `$despiked` | `spectra - cosmic_rays` | Cosmic-ray removal only. |
| `$baseline_corrected` | `spectra - baseline` | Remove the background only. |
| `$reconstruction` | `baseline + cosmic_rays + noise + peaks` | Reconstructed input. |
| `$residual` | `spectra - reconstruction` | Numerical zero for standard; an assessment of closure for ensemble. |

```{r results-selection}
length(files_components)
files_components$length
files_first <- files_components[1]
files_subset <- files_components[c(1, 3)]
dim(files_subset$corrected)
stopifnot(identical(files_components$corrected, files_components$peaks))
```

R indices start at **1**. `result[i]` selects spectra and returns another
component object; it is not list-field selection. Component and derived
fields are selected with `$` or `[[`. Subsetting retains the corresponding
names, positions and scaling metadata, and removes the original complete-grid
shape because a subset need not form the same regular map.

## Map arrays and integrated bands

`as_map(result, "peaks")` returns an array with dimensions
`c(map_shape, spectral_length)`. It requires a regular grid. Use any stored
component or derived field, such as `"baseline"` or `"corrected"`.
`band_image(result, lo, hi, component = "peaks")` integrates the selected
component by the trapezoidal rule between the inclusive axis limits. It
returns a grid for a map, or one value per spectrum otherwise.

```{r results-maps}
files_peaks_map <- as_map(files_components, "peaks")
files_baseline_map <- as_map(files_components, "baseline")
files_band <- band_image(files_components, 900, 1100)
dim(files_peaks_map)
files_band
```

Band integration requires an axis. The integration points are ordered by
increasing axis value, so descending file axes are handled consistently.
The limits may be given in either order. There must be at least one included
point; an interval containing only one point has zero trapezoidal area.
Coordinates, when available, place spectra at their physical grid locations;
otherwise the recorded native R or imported map-order convention is used.

## Plots

`plot(result, index = 1)` and `plot_components(result, index = 1)` show the
input and four component panels using base R graphics. The input panel also
shows the baseline. A stored axis is used automatically; an explicit
`wavenumbers` argument can override it. `title` changes the figure title.

```{r results-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=7}
plot(files_components, index = 1, title = "Example spectrum and RADAR components")
```

For synthetic spectra with known targets, `plot_comparison()` overlays the
true and predicted components. Such a comparison is meaningful only when
the truth and prediction use the same intensity scale:

```{r results-truth-comparison, eval=FALSE}
test_set <- generate(2, length = 128, seed = 12)
predicted <- RADAR::decompose(test_set$X, model = files_model,
                              normalize = FALSE)
plot_comparison(test_set, predicted, index = 1)
```

# Saving decompositions, spectra and datasets

`save_components(result, path)` is the convenience form of
`RADAR::write(result, path)`. `save_spectra(path, spectra, ...)` uses a
path-first argument order; `write(obj, path, ...)` uses the object first.
`save_dataset()` and `load_dataset()` retain known synthetic targets and
generation parameters. Omitting a dataset extension appends `.npz`, which
requires `jsonlite`; an explicit `.rds` is a base-R alternative.

| Output | How a decomposition is represented |
| --- | --- |
| `.rds` | Native spectral record containing input, four components, axis and metadata. |
| `.npz`, `.h5`/`.nc`, `.mat`, `.json` | Separate arrays for input and each component, plus the supported axis, names, coordinates and metadata. |
| `.csv`, `.tsv`, `.txt`, `.parquet`, `.feather`, `.db` | A tidy table: `spectrum`, optional `name`/coordinates, `wavenumber`, `spectra`, `baseline`, `cosmic_rays`, `noise`, `peaks`. |
| `.xlsx` | One wide sheet per array for ordinary decompositions; one tidy sheet for maps/coordinate records or explicit long layout. |
| `.spc`, `.jdx` and other JCAMP extensions, `.npy` | Five companion files, suffixed `_spectra`, `_baseline`, `_cosmic_rays`, `_noise`, `_peaks`; `write()` returns their paths as a character vector. |

Plain rectangular spectra usually use wide text and Excel output. Text uses
a long layout for coordinates, ragged data, multiple arrays, or when the
spectrum count is at least the channel count; the latter avoids a short-table
orientation ambiguity. Parquet, Feather and SQLite default to long tables.
`layout = "wide"` or `"long"` overrides table output where appropriate.
Wide layout requires one rectangular array; it cannot hold all decomposition
components together. Other useful writer options are `decimal` for text and
`table`/`if_exists = "replace"`, `"append"` or `"fail"` for SQLite.

Rich containers and RDS preserve model/scaling metadata. Text tables retain
their explicit axis, values, names and coordinates, but do not serialize all
model/provenance metadata. SPC and JCAMP carry their own limited format
metadata; NPY has no record metadata. Choose a rich container or RDS for an
analysis archive, and inspect the limits of the exchange format before
expecting a lossless round trip.

```{r files-save-reload}
files_result_rds <- file.path(files_dir, "components.rds")
save_components(files_components, files_result_rds)
files_reloaded <- load_components(files_result_rds)
stopifnot(identical(files_reloaded$peaks, files_components$peaks))

RADAR::write(files_components, file.path(files_dir, "components.csv"))
RADAR::write(files_X, file.path(files_dir, "plain-spectra.csv"),
             wavenumbers = files_axis, names = files_data$names)
files_small_set <- generate(2, length = 32, seed = 7)
save_dataset(files_small_set, file.path(files_dir, "known-targets.rds"))
files_restored_set <- load_dataset(file.path(files_dir, "known-targets.rds"))
```

```{r files-optional-save}
if (requireNamespace("jsonlite", quietly = TRUE)) {
  RADAR::write(files_components, file.path(files_dir, "components.json"))
  RADAR::write(files_components, file.path(files_dir, "components.npz"))
  RADAR::write(files_components, file.path(files_dir, "components.mat"))
}
if (all(vapply(c("openxlsx", "jsonlite"), requireNamespace,
               logical(1), quietly = TRUE))) {
  RADAR::write(files_components, file.path(files_dir, "components.xlsx"))
}
if (all(vapply(c("arrow", "jsonlite"), requireNamespace,
               logical(1), quietly = TRUE))) {
  RADAR::write(files_small_set, file.path(files_dir, "known-targets.parquet"))
}
```

For single-array formats, pass **any one** companion file to
`load_components()` and it locates the other four by suffix. All five must
remain together, with consistent names. Loading split NPY components cannot
recover an axis that NPY never stored.

```{r files-split-components}
files_split <- save_components(files_components,
                                file.path(files_dir, "split-components.jdx"))
basename(files_split)
files_from_split <- load_components(files_split[1])
stopifnot(max(abs(files_from_split$peaks - files_components$peaks)) < 1e-10)
```

## Converting formats



# The Rscript command-line interface

The package supplies `exec/radar.R`. Locate the installed script from R:

```{r cli-locate}
files_cli <- system.file("exec", "radar.R", package = "RADAR")
stopifnot(nzchar(files_cli))
files_cli
```

Run it as `Rscript /path/to/RADAR/exec/radar.R COMMAND ...`, or invoke the
same parser in an R session with `radar_cli(c("COMMAND", ...))`. The shell
examples below use `RADAR_CLI` as the script path; replace the illustrative
path with the installed path printed above. They are not run during vignette
building and assume you provide the named input files.

```bash
RADAR_CLI="/path/to/RADAR/exec/radar.R"
Rscript "$RADAR_CLI" --help
Rscript "$RADAR_CLI" formats
Rscript "$RADAR_CLI" info
Rscript "$RADAR_CLI" info ensemble
Rscript "$RADAR_CLI" info tuned.rds
```

`-h`/`--help` displays the shared command help. Options use separate tokens,
for example `--length 128`, rather than `--length=128`. The short aliases
are `-o` for `--output`, `-m` for `--model`, `-a` for `--architecture`, and
`-n` for `--n`. Numeric sheet indices are one based. Unknown options, missing
values, absent input files or missing required outputs produce errors; the
script exits with a nonzero status on failure.

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `decompose` | Read one or more files, estimate components and save them. |
| `convert` | Convert spectra or saved components between formats. |
| `generate` | Write synthetic spectra and all four targets. |
| `train` | Train a new native R network or fine-tune an existing one. |
| `evaluate` | Print component error metrics or summaries on a saved target dataset. |
| `formats` | Print supported adapters, extensions and optional R package requirements. |
| `info` | Print the installed RADAR/R information and bundled model information, or information about a named/saved model. |

## Decomposing files and collections

```text
Rscript radar.R decompose INPUT [INPUT ...] -o OUTPUT
    [-m ensemble|standard|MODEL.rds] [--architecture standard|ensemble]
    [--units original|normalized] [--no-normalize] [--batch-size 32]
    [READ OPTIONS] [--out-layout wide|long]
```

The default model is ensemble. `--architecture` supplies the architecture
to validate a saved RDS model. `--no-normalize` disables input scaling. Output format follows
the output extension.

```bash
Rscript "$RADAR_CLI" decompose sample.wdf -o sample_components.rds
Rscript "$RADAR_CLI" decompose spectrum.txt -o spectrum_components.csv -m standard
Rscript "$RADAR_CLI" decompose data/*.spc -o "results/{stem}_components.parquet"
Rscript "$RADAR_CLI" decompose run1.spc run2.spc -o results
Rscript "$RADAR_CLI" decompose maps.h5 --key data -o map_components.npz -m tuned.rds
Rscript "$RADAR_CLI" decompose export.csv --decimal , --layout long -o out.db
```

Shell wildcards such as `data/*.spc` are expanded by the shell. When calling
`radar_cli()` directly from R, expand them with `Sys.glob()`:

```{r cli-multiple-r, eval=FALSE}
radar_cli(c("decompose", Sys.glob("data/*.spc"),
             "-o", "results/{stem}_components.csv", "-m", "standard"))
```

The CLI expects one writable decomposition per input. For ragged inputs,
use `decompose()` in R and save each returned component object separately.
`--out-layout wide` cannot hold a five-array decomposition in a single table;
use long layout or a format that splits components.

## Reader and output options

These reader options apply to `decompose` and the spectral-reader fallback
of `convert`:

| Option | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--format NAME` | Input adapter name or extension, such as `csv`, `spc` or `jcamp`; it does not set the output format. |
| `--layout auto|wide|columns|rows|long` | Input table layout. |
| `--key NAME` | Spectral array in HDF5, NPZ, MATLAB or JSON. |
| `--sheet NAME` | Excel sheet name, numeric one-based index, or `all`. |
| `--table NAME` | SQLite table. |
| `--query SQL` | SQL returning the desired spectral table. Quote the SQL for the shell. |
| `--delimiter C` | Text separator, for example `--delimiter ";"`. |
| `--decimal .|,` | Text decimal mark. |
| `--out-layout wide|long` | Output table layout; independent of the input layout. |

The R API exposes `comments`, `skip_header` and `encoding` for text input;
these three options are not exposed by the CLI.

## Converting files

```text
Rscript radar.R convert INPUT OUTPUT [READ OPTIONS] [--out-layout wide|long]
```

```bash
Rscript "$RADAR_CLI" convert measurement.spc measurement.jdx
Rscript "$RADAR_CLI" convert map.wdf map.parquet
Rscript "$RADAR_CLI" convert result.rds result.xlsx
Rscript "$RADAR_CLI" convert export.csv clean.tsv --decimal , --out-layout long
```

This inexpensive executable example converts the temporary input created in
the vignette:

```{r cli-convert-example}
files_cli_output <- file.path(files_dir, "cli-converted.jdx")
radar_cli(c("convert", files_csv, files_cli_output))
stopifnot(file.exists(files_cli_output))
```

## Generating known-target datasets

```text
Rscript radar.R generate -n N -o OUTPUT [--length 1024] [--seed 0]
    [--train] [--min-width W] [--max-width W]
```

Defaults follow the test generator: length 1024, minimum width 10, maximum
width 300, up to 10 peaks and increased noise. `--train` switches to minimum
width 5, maximum width 256, at most 5 peaks and no increased-noise mode.
Explicit `--min-width`/`--max-width` override those widths. The CLI's default
seed is 0. Choose a multi-array format to keep all known targets together.

```bash
Rscript "$RADAR_CLI" generate -n 1000 -o test.rds
Rscript "$RADAR_CLI" generate -n 5000 --length 1340 --train -o my_train.npz
Rscript "$RADAR_CLI" generate -n 100 --length 750 --min-width 8 --max-width 120 --seed 12 -o test.h5
```

```{r cli-generate-example}
files_cli_dataset <- file.path(files_dir, "cli-targets.rds")
radar_cli(c("generate", "-n", "2", "--length", "32", "--seed", "0",
             "-o", files_cli_dataset))
stopifnot(nrow(load_dataset(files_cli_dataset)$X) == 2)
```

## Training and fine-tuning from the command line

```text
Rscript radar.R train -o MODEL.rds [-a ensemble|standard]
    [--init pretrained|MODEL.rds] [--data DATASET]
    [--epochs 10] [--steps 1000] [--batch-size 1] [--length 750]
    [--learning-rate LR] [--validation-size 1000]
    [--checkpoint BEST.rds] [--seed 0] [--verbose 1]
```

Without `--data`, each training step generates a fresh synthetic batch.
With a saved dataset, complete dataset batches determine steps per epoch.
`--init pretrained` fine-tunes the selected bundled architecture;
`--init FILE` starts from a saved RDS model. Without initialization,
the model is newly initialized. Retain a model after training with `-o`.
Omitting `--learning-rate` uses the original 12-level learning-rate schedule;
a small explicit rate such as `1e-5` is suitable for a fine-tuning experiment.
`--checkpoint` saves the best model by validation loss, or training loss if
validation is disabled.

```bash
# Small interface smoke run, not a scientifically trained model.
Rscript "$RADAR_CLI" train -a standard --epochs 1 --steps 1 --batch-size 1 --length 64 --validation-size 0 -o smoke.rds

# Fine-tune on a dataset, using a small learning rate.
Rscript "$RADAR_CLI" train -a standard --init pretrained --data my_train.npz --epochs 5 --learning-rate 1e-5 --checkpoint best.rds -o tuned.rds
```

The R training API offers additional generator settings, callbacks,
validation datasets and model-size controls; see the training section for
those workflows. The CLI does not expose every R function argument.

## Evaluation, formats and model information

```text
Rscript radar.R evaluate DATASET [-m ensemble|standard|MODEL.rds] [--statistics]
Rscript radar.R formats
Rscript radar.R info [MODEL.rds|standard|ensemble]
```

```bash
Rscript "$RADAR_CLI" evaluate test.rds -m standard
Rscript "$RADAR_CLI" evaluate test.rds -m tuned.rds --statistics
Rscript "$RADAR_CLI" formats
Rscript "$RADAR_CLI" info tuned.rds
```

`evaluate` expects a dataset containing all four true components, and prints
R lists of RMSE, MAE, maximum error and R-squared for each component.
`--statistics` instead prints means, medians and variances of per-spectrum
RMSE and maximum error. The output is printed R tables.
The current evaluation CLI uses its default prediction batch size and does
not forward a supplied `--batch-size`; use `evaluate()` in R for that control.
# Models and the scientific method

For diagrams and detailed layer shapes, see the companion
[architecture guide](architectures.html), also available with
`vignette("architectures", package = "RADAR")`.

## The two architectures

Both RADAR networks take normalized single-channel spectra and return four
components in the fixed order given by `COMPONENTS`: `baseline`, `cosmic_rays`,
`noise`, and `peaks`. In R, a spectral matrix has one spectrum per row. The
low-level `predict()` method also accepts a batch-by-points-by-one array and
always returns a named list of four matrices with the input's spectral length.
The networks operate on sample indices; they do not use the wavenumber axis as
a model input.

| Architecture | Default hidden channels (`scaler`) | Key dimension (`dim_red_size`) | Parameters | Noise and reconstruction |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|:--|
| `standard` | 20 | 256 | 585,299 | Noise is the input minus the other three components; reconstruction is additive to numerical precision. |
| `ensemble` | 10 | 144 | 280,592 | A second stage predicts noise directly with a tanh head; reconstruction can differ from the input. |

The common building blocks are:

1. **Encoder.** A one-dimensional convolution of width 128 produces `scaler`
   feature channels. Batch normalization and LeakyReLU, with negative slope
   0.3, follow the convolution.
2. **Learned key and global context.** A width-64 convolution of the encoder
   features produces `D = dim_red_size` channels. Global max pooling over the
   spectrum gives a learned key vector of length `D`. The outer product of the
   signal of length `L` with that key forms an `L` by `D` map. Two
   two-dimensional convolutions, with kernel sizes `c(32, floor(D / 10))` and
   `c(16, floor(D / 10))` and strides `c(1, sqrt(D))`, reduce the key dimension
   to one while preserving the spectral length. This gives every position
   information about the whole spectrum.
3. **Decoder.** After reshaping to one-dimensional features, convolutions of
   widths 128 and 64, each followed by batch normalization and LeakyReLU,
   produce the features used by the component heads.

There are two different padding rules. One-dimensional convolutions and
average-pooling operations extend the input by repeating its first and last
values, then apply a valid operation. A window of size `k` gets `floor(k / 2)`
extra values on the left and `floor(k / 2) - 1 + k %% 2` on the right. These
asymmetric counts for even windows preserve the original alignment. The
strided **two-dimensional** convolutions use zero padding with the usual
`same` rule. They do not use edge repetition.

| Head | Main operations | Purpose |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Baseline | Width-64 convolution; average pooling of width 33; ReLU | Broad, smooth background |
| Cosmic rays | Width-3 convolution; ReLU | Very narrow, often one- or two-point spikes |
| Peaks | Width-8 convolution; average pooling of width 4; ReLU | Raman bands with sharp features retained |
| Noise, standard | Input minus baseline, cosmic rays and peaks | Exact additive remainder |
| Noise, ensemble | Width-1 convolution; tanh | Independently estimated signed noise |

In the standard network, the baseline and peak convolutions also have a ReLU
before pooling. In the ensemble, their ReLU follows pooling. Hidden kernels
use L1 and L2 penalties of `1e-6` by default; head kernels use L1 `1e-5` and
L2 `1e-6`. Biases and activities use L2 `1e-6`. Batch normalization uses epsilon
`0.001`, moving-moment coefficient `0.99`, and learned scale and shift.

The **standard** model has one encoder, key block and decoder. Its three
nonnegative heads estimate baseline, cosmic rays and peaks; noise is the
remainder. Its component loss is root mean squared error (RMSE).

The **ensemble** works in two stages. Stage 1 estimates baseline and cosmic
rays. The reduced spectrum, `input - baseline - cosmic_rays`, enters a second
encoder and learned-key block. Stage 1's second two-dimensional convolution
also supplies a residual connection to the corresponding features in stage 2.
The second decoder estimates peaks and noise. Each component uses the joined
loss `RMSE + (1 - R_squared)`. The independent noise head explains why an
ensemble decomposition can have a nonzero `$residual`; that behavior is part
of the published architecture.

```{r models-load-native}
library(RADAR)
models_standard <- load_model("standard")
models_ensemble <- load_pretrained("ensemble")
models_standard
models_ensemble
COMPONENTS
```

Raw `predict()` does not normalize its input or restore intensity units. Use
it when the values already have the desired network scale; use
`RADAR::decompose(..., model = model)` when preprocessing and unit restoration
are needed. Its defaults are `batch_size = 32` and `verbose = 0`. The native
prediction method evaluates spectra individually to bound attention memory,
even when a larger batch size is supplied. A map cube should first be passed
to the high-level decomposition interface, since the third dimension of the
low-level prediction array means the single channel.

```{r models-raw-prediction}
models_input <- matrix(seq(0, 1, length.out = 32), nrow = 1)
models_raw <- predict(models_standard, models_input, batch_size = 1, verbose = 0)
vapply(models_raw, ncol, integer(1))
max(abs(Reduce(`+`, models_raw) - models_input))
```

## Building a network of another size

`build_model()`, `build_standard_model()`, `build_ensemble_model()` and
`new_model()` create randomly initialized native `radar_model` objects.
`dim_red_size` must be a perfect square of at least 16; `scaler` is a positive
integer. `l1_param`, `l2_param`, `seed` and `name` control regularization,
initialization and naming. The pretrained weights fit the default dimensions
only. A different channel count or key dimension needs newly trained weights.

```{r models-custom-size}
models_small <- new_model("standard", scaler = 2, dim_red_size = 16,
                          l1_param = 1e-6, l2_param = 1e-6, seed = 3)
models_small$n_parameters
models_small$hyperparameters

# More control over the same native model representation:
models_small <- compile_model(models_small, learning_rate = 1e-5)
```

`compile_model()` records the learning-rate setting. `train()` configures its
own optimizer for each training call. The R
model has no underlying `$model` that must be accessed to make it work.
`print(model)`, `$architecture`, `$hyperparameters`, `$n_parameters`, `$weights`,
`$history`, `$training` and `model_info()` expose its structure and provenance.

## Bundled pretrained models

`inst/weights/standard.rds` and `inst/weights/ensemble.rds` contain complete
native models. `load_model()` reads the installed objects directly.
Each model was trained on 240 million synthetic spectra of length 750:
12 epochs, 200,000 batches per epoch and 100 spectra per batch. Training
used band widths from 5 to 255 samples and the twelve-level schedule below.
The bundled numerical regression fixtures cover both architectures and all
four components at spectral lengths 1,024 and 1,738, with tolerance `1e-5`.

## Model persistence and software information

`load_model("standard")` and `load_model("ensemble")` load pretrained models.
Passing an existing `radar_model` returns it. `save_model()` writes the native
R representation using RDS. It records the architecture, hyperparameters,
weights, parameter count, origin, training record and history, plus the RADAR
version, R version, platform and UTC save date. It creates missing parent
directories. Use `overwrite = FALSE` to protect an existing model file.

```{r models-save-and-inspect}
models_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
save_model(models_small, models_file)
models_reloaded <- load_model(models_file)
models_info <- model_info(models_file)
models_info[c("architecture", "hyperparameters", "n_parameters", "saved_with")]
unlink(models_file)
```

`model_info(model_or_path, show = TRUE)` prints a readable summary and returns
a list. For a trained model, `$training` includes epoch and batch settings,
learning-rate description, spectra seen and final loss; fine-tuning preserves
the earlier record under `$training$started_from`. Checkpoint metadata is
updated before the checkpoint is saved, so it describes those checkpoint
weights. Native RDS files do **not** preserve Adam moments for exact optimizer
continuation: every call to `train()` starts fresh optimizer state.

# Synthetic spectra and known component targets

## Component distributions

Synthetic spectra make supervised training possible because all four true
components are available separately. The R generator follows the original
scientific distributions:

| Component | Distribution before final mixture scaling |
|:--|:--|
| Baseline | A random subset of five elementary backgrounds: linear, sinusoidal, polynomial, Gaussian and Lorentzian. Each of the five is independently included or omitted, and included curves add together. |
| Cosmic rays | A uniformly drawn integer from 0 through 29 spikes, with positions sampled across the spectrum and heights uniform on `[0, 1)`. Repeated positions are overwritten in draw order. |
| Noise | White Gaussian noise with standard deviation drawn uniformly from `[0, 0.1)`; the first and last samples are set to zero. |
| Peaks | Between 1 and `max_num_peaks - 1` bands; integer widths are drawn from `[min_width, max_width)`. Gaussian, Lorentzian and Voigt profiles each have approximately one-third probability, random heights and random locations. Overlapping profiles add; the final peak spectrum is normalized to a maximum close to one and its endpoints are zero. |

The elementary baselines are drawn over a coordinate from zero to one.
The linear background has two independently uniform endpoints. The sine has
random phase and stretch, with maximum periodicity controlled by
`sin_max_periodicity = 8`. The polynomial degree is an integer from 2 to 10 by
default. Gaussian and Lorentzian centers lie near one end, in `[0, 0.2]` or
`[0.8, 1]`; signs, widths, scaling and offsets vary. Normalization, scaling and
shifting keep each elementary curve within `[0, 1]` before summing the subset.

An individual band is evaluated over `[-extremity, extremity]`, with default
`extremity = 0.5`. Gaussian bands use an integer radial-basis parameter from
5 through 9; Lorentzian widths are uniform from 0.1 to 0.3. Voigt profiles use
Gaussian width `sigma` uniform from 0.01 to 0.3 and Lorentzian width `gamma`
uniform from 0 to 0.1. The implementation selects Gaussian for a uniform draw
below 0.33, Lorentzian from 0.33 to below 0.66, and Voigt otherwise; their
probabilities are 0.33, 0.33 and 0.34. A separate uniform height scales each
band. Voigt profiles use a native complex rational approximation to the
complex probability function; SciPy is not required.

`generate_sample()` draws three integer weights from 0 through 9 for baseline,
cosmic rays and peaks, then divides them by their sum. It redraws an all-zero
weight vector or a mixture with zero maximum. Noise is added after the
signal-component mixture and uses the peak component's mixture weight.

| Setting | Argument | Scaling and noise |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Training | `increase_noise = FALSE` | Divide the signal components by the mixture maximum; scale noise by the peak weight; set noise to zero in 5% of samples. With consistent scaling, the input is the sum of the normalized targets. |
| Test | `increase_noise = TRUE` | Multiply noise by an integer from 3 through 9 and by the peak weight; min-max normalize the noisy mixture to `[0, 1]`. The baseline absorbs the subtracted minimum, preserving additivity. |

Band width is expressed in **points**, not inverse centimeters. For spectra
shorter than 500 points, `generate_spectrum()` overrides the requested band
widths with lower bound `max(floor(length / 32), 1)` and exclusive upper bound
`max(floor(length / 2), lower_bound + 1)`, matching the original short-spectrum
rule. This also applies when `generate_sample()` or `generate_dataset()`
calls it. Width options supplied for a short example therefore do not change
that rule.

## Finite datasets and default settings

`generate()` is an alias for `generate_dataset()`. Both return a
`synthetic_dataset` with `$X` (also `$spectra`), `$baseline`, `$cosmic_rays`,
`$noise`, `$peaks` and `$params`. Each array is spectra by points. `$targets`
is a named list in `COMPONENTS` order, `$n_spectra` is the number of spectra,
and `$length` is the number of points. `length(dataset)` counts spectra;
`dataset[i]` selects rows while retaining a dataset object.

| Interface | Length | Width bounds | `max_num_peaks` | `increase_noise` | Other defaults |
|:--|--:|:--|--:|:--|:--|
| `generate()` / `generate_dataset()` | 1024 | `[10, 300)` | 10 | `TRUE` | `seed = NULL`, consistent scaling |
| `generate_sample()` | 1024 | `[5, 256)` | 10 | `FALSE` | `rng = NULL`, consistent scaling |
| `batch_generator()` | 750 | `[5, 256)` | 5 | `FALSE` | `batch_size = 100`, `seed = NULL` |
| Synthetic data inside `train()` | 750 | `[5, 256)` | 5 | `FALSE` | Native default `batch_size = 1`, `seed = 0` |

The upper peak-count bound is exclusive: `max_num_peaks = 5` means one to four
bands. `max_num_peaks <= 1` produces one band. The upper width bound is also
exclusive. Elementary component functions have their own defaults, so pass
explicit bounds when calling them directly.

```{r synthetic-finite-data}
synthetic_demo <- generate_dataset(4, length = 128, seed = 17)
dim(synthetic_demo$X)
names(synthetic_demo$targets)
synthetic_demo$params
length(synthetic_demo[1:2])
max(abs(synthetic_demo$X - Reduce(`+`, synthetic_demo$targets)))
```

`as_training_data()` produces `list(X, targets)`, with `$X` shaped
`c(n_spectra, length, 1)` and four target matrices. These remain native R
arrays in double precision.

```{r synthetic-training-arrays}
synthetic_arrays <- as_training_data(synthetic_demo)
dim(synthetic_arrays$X)
vapply(synthetic_arrays$targets, ncol, integer(1))
```

`train_test_datasets()` creates independent training and testing streams. Its
training defaults are widths 5--256, at most four peaks, and normal noise;
testing defaults are widths 10--300, at most nine peaks, and amplified noise.
`train_kwargs` and `test_kwargs` are lists that override these defaults.

```{r synthetic-independent-splits}
synthetic_split <- train_test_datasets(
  n_train = 4, n_test = 2, length = 64, seed = 23,
  train_kwargs = list(max_num_peaks = 5),
  test_kwargs = list(max_num_peaks = 5)
)
synthetic_split$train$params$increase_noise
synthetic_split$test$params$increase_noise
```

Datasets can be saved and reloaded through `save_dataset()` and
`load_dataset()` using a multi-array format. For example, an RDS round trip
uses no optional format dependencies:

```{r synthetic-save-dataset}
synthetic_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
save_dataset(synthetic_split$train, synthetic_file)
synthetic_restored <- load_dataset(synthetic_file)
stopifnot(identical(synthetic_restored$X, synthetic_split$train$X))
unlink(synthetic_file)
```

## Streams, single samples and component-level control

`batch_generator()` returns a function with its own advancing random stream.
Each call generates a fresh batch and returns `$X`, `$targets` and `$dataset`.
It is an R
closure.

```{r synthetic-batch-stream}
synthetic_next <- batch_generator(length = 64, batch_size = 2, seed = 31)
synthetic_batch_one <- synthetic_next()
synthetic_batch_two <- synthetic_next()
dim(synthetic_batch_one$X)
identical(synthetic_batch_one$X, synthetic_batch_two$X)
```

The lower-level functions allow components to be studied separately:

```{r synthetic-components}
synthetic_sample <- generate_sample(length = 64, rng = 41,
                                    increase_noise = FALSE)
synthetic_background <- generate_baseline(64, rng = 42)
synthetic_bands <- generate_peaks(64, max_num_peaks = 6,
                                min_peak_width = 3, max_peak_width = 15, rng = 43)
synthetic_spikes <- generate_cosmic_rays(64, max_num = 10, rng = 44)
synthetic_noise <- generate_noise(64, scaling_factor = 0.1, rng = 45)
synthetic_elementary <- make_baselines(64, rng = 46)
synthetic_one_band <- get_random_peak(length = 16, rng = 47)
synthetic_unscaled <- generate_spectrum(64, rng = 48)
names(synthetic_unscaled)
```

`generate_spectrum()` returns the four **unscaled** components.
`generate_sample()` returns `$spectrum` and `$targets` after mixture weighting
and the selected scaling rule. `make_baselines()` exposes the five background
curves; `get_random_peak()` produces one band. `generate_noise()` accepts
`scaling_factor`, and `generate_cosmic_rays()` accepts the exclusive count
bound `max_num`.

## Reproducibility and legacy scaling

Supply `seed` to finite datasets or streams and `rng` to single-sample and
component functions for reproducible R draws. Seeded generator calls restore
the caller's R random state; each seeded batch closure maintains its own
state between calls. With `seed = NULL` or `rng = NULL`, the current R random
state is used. `train()` and
model initialization have their own seed arguments; the generator's
state-preservation guarantee does not imply that training leaves the caller's
random state untouched.

```{r synthetic-reproducible-seeds}
synthetic_same <- generate_dataset(4, length = 128, seed = 17)
stopifnot(identical(synthetic_demo$X, synthetic_same$X))
```

RADAR uses consistent scaling by default. Set `legacy_scaling = TRUE` to
reproduce the original training-input rule. This option exists on
`generate_sample()`, `generate_dataset()`, `batch_generator()` and `train()`;
it affects only `increase_noise = FALSE`. The pretrained models were trained
with the legacy rule. The amplified-noise test setting was already consistent
and is unchanged.

```{r synthetic-legacy-scaling}
synthetic_legacy <- generate_sample(128, rng = 51, legacy_scaling = TRUE)
synthetic_consistent <- generate_sample(128, rng = 51, legacy_scaling = FALSE)
c(legacy_difference = max(abs(synthetic_legacy$spectrum -
                                Reduce(`+`, synthetic_legacy$targets))),
  consistent_difference = max(abs(synthetic_consistent$spectrum -
                                    Reduce(`+`, synthetic_consistent$targets))))
```

# Training and fine-tuning in R

## What is optimized

Native reverse-mode differentiation covers every convolution, learned key,
outer product, pooling operation, batch-normalization scale and shift,
residual connection, and component head. Global-max ties share their
derivative equally. Batch normalization computes minibatch/spatial statistics
and updates its moving moments during training; inference uses the moving
moments. Adam uses `beta1 = 0.9`, `beta2 = 0.999` and epsilon `1e-7`, with the
epsilon added to the uncorrected second-moment denominator.

The component loss is RMSE for `standard`, or RMSE plus `1 - R_squared` for
`ensemble`. Component losses are summed and kernel, bias and activity
regularization is added. Validation uses inference-mode normalization and
includes regularization. The exported helpers
`root_mean_squared_error()`, `r_square()`, `r_square_loss()` and
`joined_loss()` expose the training formulas. These operate over all values
of the supplied batch; their stabilized `R_squared` denominator uses
`1e-7`. They serve a different purpose from per-spectrum reporting metrics.

Calling `train(model = "standard")` or `train(model = "ensemble")` with
`init = NULL` creates a **new random network**. In contrast,
`load_model("standard")` returns pretrained weights. To fine-tune, supply
`init = "pretrained"`, an existing model object, or a saved model through
`init`. Always retain the returned model: native R objects are not updated by
reference.

## Training options and native defaults

| Argument | Native R default | Meaning |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `data` | `NULL` | Fresh synthetic batches; alternatively a dataset, `list(X, targets)`, or a dataset path. |
| `model` | `"ensemble"` | Architecture for new weights, or an existing `radar_model`. |
| `init` | `NULL` | Random initialization; use `"pretrained"` or a saved model path to start elsewhere. An existing `model` object takes precedence. |
| `save_to` | `NULL` | Save the final model to an RDS file. |
| `epochs` | 10 | Passes over fixed data, or synthetic-stream epochs. |
| `steps_per_epoch` | 1000 | Synthetic batches per epoch; ignored for a fixed dataset. |
| `batch_size` | 1 | Spectra in one optimizer step. |
| `learning_rate` | `"original"` | Original twelve-level schedule stretched to this run; a positive constant or an R function of zero-based step is also accepted. |
| `length`, `min_width`, `max_width`, `max_num_peaks` | 750, 5, 256, 5 | Synthetic-training geometry; count and upper width bounds are exclusive. |
| `increase_noise`, `legacy_scaling` | `FALSE`, `FALSE` | Synthetic-training noise and input-scaling rules. |
| `validation_data` | `NULL` | No validation by default; alternatively `"synthetic"`, a dataset, an array/target list, or a dataset path. |
| `validation_size`, `validation_length` | 100, 2000 | Number and length when generating synthetic validation data. |
| `seed` | 0 | Initialization and training randomness; `NULL` retains current random state. |
| `callbacks` | `NULL` | List of native R functions called after each epoch. |
| `checkpoint_path` | `NULL` | RDS file retaining the epoch with the lowest monitored loss. |
| `verbose` | 1 | Print epoch losses; use 0 for quiet execution. |

For **fixed data**, each epoch shuffles the rows and visits every spectrum.
The number of optimizer steps is `ceiling(n_spectra / batch_size)` per epoch.
Targets may be an unnamed list in `COMPONENTS` order or a named list with
those four component names. Each target must be a finite matrix matching
`X`; a `c(n_spectra, length, 1)` input array is also accepted.

## A small fixed-data training run

The following is an executable demonstration with a small network and four
short training spectra. Its purpose is to show the workflow, not to establish
an accurate new model.

```{r training-fixed-small}
training_initial <- new_model("standard", scaler = 2, dim_red_size = 16,
                              seed = 61)
training_fit <- train(synthetic_split$train, model = training_initial,
                      epochs = 2, batch_size = 2, learning_rate = 1e-5,
                      validation_data = synthetic_split$test,
                      seed = 62, verbose = 0)
training_fit$history$loss
training_fit$history$val_loss
training_fit$history$component_loss
```

`$history$component_loss` is an epoch-by-component matrix. `$history$loss`
includes regularization; the separate component matrix does not.
`$history$val_loss` is `NULL` when validation is disabled. A model can also be
trained on plain arrays:

```{r training-array-data, eval=FALSE}
training_from_arrays <- train(
  list(synthetic_split$train$X, synthetic_split$train$targets),
  model = new_model("standard", scaler = 2, dim_red_size = 16, seed = 61),
  epochs = 1, batch_size = 2, learning_rate = 1e-5, verbose = 0
)
```

## Synthetic-stream training

A short native stream run is equally explicit:

```{r training-stream-small}
training_stream <- train(
  data = NULL,
  model = new_model("standard", scaler = 2, dim_red_size = 16, seed = 63),
  epochs = 1, steps_per_epoch = 2, batch_size = 1, length = 64,
  max_num_peaks = 5, increase_noise = FALSE,
  validation_data = NULL, learning_rate = 1e-5, seed = 64, verbose = 0
)
training_stream$training[c("epochs", "steps_per_epoch", "batch_size",
                            "spectra_seen", "final_loss")]
```

```{r training-original-full-schedule, eval=FALSE}
training_full <- train(
  model = "ensemble", epochs = 12, steps_per_epoch = 200000,
  batch_size = 100, length = 750, min_width = 5, max_width = 256,
  max_num_peaks = 5, increase_noise = FALSE, legacy_scaling = TRUE,
  learning_rate = "original",
  validation_data = "synthetic", validation_size = 1000,
  validation_length = 2000, checkpoint_path = "best_original.rds",
  save_to = "trained_original.rds", seed = 0
)
```

## Learning-rate schedules

`ORIGINAL_LR_VALUES` contains the original levels:

`0.00105, 0.00075, 0.00045, 0.00015, 0.000105, 0.000075, 0.000045,
0.000015, 0.0000105, 0.0000075, 0.0000045, 0.0000015`.

The original run held each level for approximately 200,000 optimizer steps.
`original_learning_rate_schedule(total_steps)` places the eleven boundaries
at rounded multiples of `total_steps / 12`, retaining the original
piecewise-constant boundary convention. Runs shorter than twelve steps use
the first level throughout. `train(learning_rate = "original")` computes the
total number of steps from the stream settings or fixed dataset and uses
this schedule.

```{r training-schedule-functions}
training_schedule <- original_learning_rate_schedule(total_steps = 120)
training_steps <- c(0, 11, 21, 61, 111)
data.frame(step = training_steps,
           learning_rate = vapply(training_steps, training_schedule, numeric(1)))

# Any positive-valued R function of the zero-based optimizer step can be used.
training_custom_schedule <- function(step) 1e-5 / (1 + step / 100)
training_custom_schedule(0)
```

## Checkpoints, callbacks and continuation

`checkpoint_path` saves the best epoch by validation loss when validation is
provided, or by training loss otherwise. `save_to` writes the final returned
model, which can differ from the best checkpoint. Epoch-end callbacks are
ordinary R functions with signature `function(epoch, model, logs)`. `logs`
contains `loss` and, when available, `val_loss`. A callback can inspect or
record progress; returning a `radar_model` replaces the current model.
These callbacks are ordinary R functions.

```{r training-checkpoints-callbacks}
training_checkpoint <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
training_callback_log <- numeric()
training_record <- function(epoch, model, logs) {
  training_callback_log <<- c(training_callback_log, logs$loss)
  invisible(NULL)
}
training_checkpoint_fit <- train(
  synthetic_split$train,
  model = new_model("standard", scaler = 2, dim_red_size = 16, seed = 65),
  epochs = 2, batch_size = 2, learning_rate = 1e-5,
  validation_data = synthetic_split$test,
  callbacks = list(training_record), checkpoint_path = training_checkpoint,
  seed = 66, verbose = 0
)
training_best <- load_model(training_checkpoint)
training_callback_log
training_best$training[c("epochs", "spectra_seen", "final_loss")]
unlink(training_checkpoint)
```

To continue from native saved weights, call `train(data, model = saved_model)`
or `train(data, model = "standard", init = "previous.rds")`. Weights and
batch-normalization moments continue from the supplied model; Adam moments
and optimizer step numbering restart. The `started_from` provenance chain
records each training invocation.

## Fine-tuning pretrained weights

Adapting a network to an instrument requires examples with **known** baseline,
cosmic-ray, noise and peak components. Synthetic spectra resembling the
instrument's sampling, band widths and noise are often the practical choice.
Keep a separate held-out test set for assessment.

The following realistic-size example is not executed during vignette builds:

```{r training-pretrained-finetune, eval=FALSE}
training_instrument <- train_test_datasets(
  n_train = 5000, n_test = 500, length = 1340, seed = 71,
  train_kwargs = list(min_width = 8, max_width = 300),
  test_kwargs = list(min_width = 8, max_width = 300)
)
training_before <- evaluate("ensemble", training_instrument$test)
training_tuned <- train(
  training_instrument$train, model = "ensemble", init = "pretrained",
  epochs = 5, batch_size = 1, learning_rate = 1e-5,
  validation_data = training_instrument$test, save_to = "instrument_tuned.rds"
)
training_after <- evaluate(training_tuned, training_instrument$test)
```

Use a small constant learning rate, such as `1e-5` or smaller, for
fine-tuning. The original schedule starts at `1.05e-3` and can quickly change
pretrained weights. Always compare held-out performance before and after.
Small training sets can make results worse because batch-normalization
statistics are re-estimated from only a few batches. Retain the pretrained
model if the tuned version is poorer.

The original models were trained on 750-point spectra with bands 5--256
points wide. A different instrument can have the same chemical bands spread
over very different numbers of samples. Resampling or targeted fine-tuning
may be useful when that geometry differs substantially. Input normalization
allows different intensity scales; it does not establish accuracy for every
instrument or spectrum.

# Evaluation, error statistics and comparisons

## Reporting metrics

`evaluate()` accepts a pretrained model name, native model path, or model
object, and a synthetic dataset or saved dataset path. It defaults to
`normalize = FALSE`, since the synthetic inputs already have their intended
network scale and the ground-truth targets use that scale. If you enable
normalization, the comparison still needs consistent target units.

For errors `e_ij = prediction_ij - truth_ij` at point `j` of spectrum `i`:

| Reported metric | Per-spectrum calculation | Summary in `evaluate()` |
|:--|:--|:--|
| RMSE | `sqrt(mean(e_i^2))` | Arithmetic mean across spectra |
| MAE | `mean(abs(e_i))` | Arithmetic mean across spectra |
| Max error | `max(abs(e_i))` | Arithmetic mean of each spectrum's worst local error |
| R squared | `1 - sum(error^2) / sum((truth - mean(truth))^2)` | Pooled across every point of every spectrum for that component |

The reported max error is not the single largest value in the entire
dataset. It averages spectrum-wise maxima. It complements RMSE: a missed
cosmic ray, clipped peak top or localized baseline bump can be important even
when its error is diluted by many correctly predicted points.

Pooled R squared avoids averaging undefined per-spectrum values for constant
components, such as spectra with no cosmic rays. It can be negative for a
poor prediction. If the pooled truth itself is constant, the reporting
function returns `NaN` when its total variation is at or below `1e-12`.

```{r evaluation-model-metrics}
evaluation_demo <- generate_dataset(2, length = 128, seed = 81)
evaluation_standard <- evaluate(models_standard, evaluation_demo)
evaluation_ensemble <- evaluate(models_ensemble, evaluation_demo)
evaluation_standard$peaks
evaluation_ensemble$peaks
```

`statistics = TRUE` returns mean, median and **population variance** across
spectra of the per-spectrum RMSE and maximum error. Variance is
`mean((x - mean(x))^2)`, rather than R's sample variance `var(x)`.

```{r evaluation-error-statistics}
evaluation_summary <- evaluate(models_standard, evaluation_demo,
                                statistics = TRUE)
evaluation_summary$noise
```

The returned component list contains `rmse_mean`, `rmse_median`,
`rmse_variance`, `max_error_mean`, `max_error_median` and
`max_error_variance`. The units of RMSE, MAE and maximum error match the
component intensities; variance has squared intensity units and R squared is
unitless.

## Low-level metrics and visual checks

`evaluate_components()` and `error_statistics()` accept datasets,
decomposition objects or ordinary named lists containing the four components.
`per_spectrum_errors()` retains the individual spectrum errors. `rmse()`,
`mae()`, `max_error()` and `r2()` reduce the final axis by default; with a
spectra-by-points matrix this gives one number per row. Set `axis = NULL` to
pool all values. R axis indices are one-based, and `axis = -1` selects the
last axis.

```{r evaluation-component-comparison, fig.height=8, fig.width=7}
evaluation_parts <- RADAR::decompose(evaluation_demo$X, model = models_standard,
                                     normalize = FALSE)
evaluation_individual <- per_spectrum_errors(evaluation_demo, evaluation_parts)
evaluation_individual$peaks
rmse(evaluation_demo$peaks, evaluation_parts$peaks)
r2(evaluation_demo$peaks, evaluation_parts$peaks, axis = NULL)
evaluate_components(evaluation_demo, evaluation_parts)$peaks
plot_comparison(evaluation_demo, evaluation_parts, index = 1)
```

`plot_comparison()` displays the input and true component curves with the
predictions overlaid as red dashed lines. `plot_components()` or
`plot(evaluation_parts, index = 1)` shows an ordinary decomposition. Plotting
uses R's standard graphics and one-based spectrum indices. Inspect a few
cases before drawing conclusions from aggregate scores. Exceptionally sharp,
intense Raman bands can be assigned partly to cosmic rays; structured noise
can leak into the peak component. A very large cosmic ray also compresses the
rest of its spectrum into a small normalized intensity range.

`snr(signal, noise, predicted_noise = 0, eps = 1e-4)` is the mean signal divided
by the population standard deviation of `noise - predicted_noise`, with `eps`
added to the denominator. Select a signal-band region and a detrended,
band-free noise region that make physical sense for your analysis.

```{r evaluation-snr-helper}
evaluation_signal_region <- c(1.0, 1.2, 1.1, 1.0)
evaluation_noise_region <- c(-0.02, 0.01, 0.02, -0.01)
snr(evaluation_signal_region, evaluation_noise_region)
```


# Complete R API reference

## The eight main functions

| R function | Inputs and result |
|---|---|
| `RADAR::decompose(spectra, model = "ensemble", output = NULL, ...)` | A vector, spectra-by-channel matrix, map array, list of spectra, spectral-data object, synthetic dataset or file becomes `radar_components`; unequal lengths produce a list of decompositions. `output` writes the result. |
| `RADAR::read(path, format = NULL, ...)` | Read a supported spectral file into a `spectral_data` record. |
| `RADAR::write(obj, path, format = NULL, wavenumbers = NULL, names = NULL, ...)` | Write a numeric array, spectral record, decomposition or synthetic dataset; return the output path or companion-file paths. |
| `formats(show = FALSE)` | Return a data frame describing adapters, extensions, read/write support and optional dependencies; `show = TRUE` prints it. |
| `load_model(model = "ensemble", architecture = NULL, compile = TRUE)` | Load a bundled architecture, native RDS model; return a native `radar_model`. Existing `radar_model` objects are accepted. |
| `train(data = NULL, model = "ensemble", init = NULL, save_to = NULL, ...)` | Train from fresh weights or fine-tune a model; return the updated `radar_model`, including history and training provenance. Retain this returned value. |
| `generate(n, length = 1024, ...)` | Alias of `generate_dataset()`; return a `synthetic_dataset` containing inputs and all four true components. |
| `evaluate(model, dataset, statistics = FALSE, normalize = FALSE, batch_size = 32)` | Evaluate a synthetic dataset or saved dataset file and return per-component metric lists; `statistics = TRUE` selects population summaries. |

## Model, file and object helpers

| Public R export | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `build_model(architecture = "ensemble", ...)` | Construct an initialized native network with a chosen architecture and hyperparameters. |
| `build_standard_model(...)` | Construct the single-stage standard architecture. |
| `build_ensemble_model(...)` | Construct the two-stage ensemble architecture. |
| `new_model(architecture = "ensemble", ...)` | Convenience entry point to `build_model()`. |
| `compile_model(model, architecture = model$architecture, learning_rate = 1e-5)` | Validate the architecture and configure the model's learning-rate setting. |
| `load_pretrained(architecture = "ensemble")` | Load one of the two bundled pretrained models. |
| `save_model(model, path, overwrite = TRUE)` | Save a native `.rds` model, weights, history and provenance. |
| `model_info(model = "ensemble", show = FALSE)` | Inspect architecture, hyperparameters, parameter count, origin, training details, saved software versions and format information. |
| `read_spectra(path, ...)` | Alias of `read()`. |
| `save_spectra(path, spectra, wavenumbers = NULL, names = NULL, ...)` | Save a numeric spectrum or matrix. The path precedes the data in this convenience function. |
| `save_components(components, path, ...)` | Save a decomposition using a supported spectral format. |
| `load_components(path, format = NULL, ...)` | Restore all four components, input spectra and supported metadata; locate companion files for single-array formats. |
| `save_dataset(dataset, path, ...)` | Save synthetic inputs and their targets; append `.npz` when the path has no extension. |
| `load_dataset(path, format = NULL, ...)` | Restore a `synthetic_dataset` from a multi-array file. |
| `spectral_data(intensities, ...)` | Construct a spectral record, optionally including named arrays, axes, spectrum names and coordinates. |
| `SpectralData(intensities, ...)` | Alias of `spectral_data()`, retained as a familiar constructor name. |
| `radar_components(spectra, baseline, cosmic_rays, noise, peaks, ...)` | Construct a decomposition with matching component shapes. Usually returned by `decompose()`. |
| `synthetic_dataset(X, baseline, cosmic_rays, noise, peaks, params = list())` | Construct a synthetic dataset from existing input and target matrices. |

## Generation, preprocessing, metrics and display

| Public R export | Purpose and result |
|---|---|
| `generate_dataset(n, length = 1024, ...)` | Finite synthetic dataset with generator parameters recorded in `$params`. |
| `generate_sample(length = 1024, ...)` | One sample as `list(spectrum = ..., targets = ...)`. |
| `generate_spectrum(length, ...)` | Named list of four unscaled components. |
| `make_baselines(length, ...)` | Five elementary backgrounds: linear, sinusoidal, polynomial, Gaussian and Lorentzian. |
| `generate_baseline(length, rng = NULL)` | Random sum of elementary background curves. |
| `get_random_peak(length = 16, extremity = 0.5, rng = NULL)` | A random Gaussian, Lorentzian or Voigt band. |
| `generate_peaks(length = 1000, ...)` | A peak-only spectrum normalized to a maximum of at most one. |
| `generate_cosmic_rays(length = 1000, max_num = 30, rng = NULL)` | Single-channel spikes. |
| `generate_noise(length = 1000, scaling_factor = 0.1, rng = NULL)` | White Gaussian noise with zero endpoints. |
| `train_test_datasets(n_train, n_test, length = 1024, seed = 0, ...)` | Named list with independent `$train` and `$test` datasets. |
| `batch_generator(length = 750, batch_size = 100, ...)` | Return a closure; each call creates the next batch with `$X`, `$targets` and `$dataset`. |
| `as_training_data(x)` | Convert a synthetic dataset to `list(X = ..., targets = ...)`; `X` has dimensions `n × length × 1`. |
| `minmax_normalize(spectra)` | Return `$normalized` and `$scaling`; scaling contains per-spectrum `$offset` and `$scale`. |
| `denormalize_components(components, scaling)` | Restore intensity units; restore the offset to baseline only. |
| `rmse(y_true, y_pred, axis = -1)` | Per-spectrum root mean squared errors. |
| `mae(y_true, y_pred, axis = -1)` | Per-spectrum mean absolute errors. |
| `max_error(y_true, y_pred, axis = -1)` | Per-spectrum maximum absolute errors. |
| `r2(y_true, y_pred, axis = -1, eps = 1e-12)` | Per-spectrum coefficients of determination; constant targets give `NaN`. |
| `per_spectrum_errors(truth, prediction)` | Nested component lists of per-spectrum RMSE, MAE and maximum error. |
| `evaluate_components(truth, prediction)` | Component summaries: average per-spectrum errors and pooled R squared. |
| `error_statistics(truth, prediction)` | Mean, median and population variance of per-spectrum RMSE and maximum error. |
| `snr(signal, noise, predicted_noise = 0, eps = 1e-4)` | Mean signal divided by the population standard deviation of residual noise, with stabilizer. |
| `root_mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred)` | Scalar neural-network RMSE loss over all supplied values. |
| `r_square(y_true, y_pred)` | Pooled neural-network R squared using the training epsilon. |
| `r_square_loss(y_true, y_pred)` | The training loss `1 - R squared`. |
| `joined_loss(y_true, y_pred)` | RMSE plus `r_square_loss()`. |
| `original_learning_rate_schedule(total_steps)` | Return a function of zero-based optimizer step using the original twelve learning-rate levels. |
| `as_map(x, component = "peaks")` | View a component as `c(map_shape, spectral_length)`; use `component = "spectra"` for a spectral record. |
| `band_image(x, lo, hi, component = "peaks")` | Trapezoidal band integrals, returned as a vector or spatial map. |
| `plot_components(components, index = 1, ...)` | Plot the input and its four components in five panels. |
| `plot_comparison(dataset, components, index = 1, ...)` | Overlay true and predicted components. |
| `radar_cli(args = commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE))` | Run the documented command-line interface from a character argument vector. |
