| `radar_citation()` | Return the method's paper reference as text. |
| `COMPONENTS` | Character constant `c("baseline", "cosmic_rays", "noise", "peaks")`; model output order. |
| `ORIGINAL_LR_VALUES` | Numeric constant containing the original twelve learning-rate levels. |

For matrix error metrics, the default `axis = -1` reduces the final, spectral
axis. Other explicit axis numbers follow R's one-based axis convention;
`axis = NULL` pools all values. The scalar training losses are distinct from
the per-spectrum metrics. See the training and evaluation sections for their
formulas and intended uses.


# Reproducibility and computational limits

Seeded generator calls restore the caller's random state. Each seeded stream
maintains its own state. Model initialization and training have their own
seed arguments. Save model objects and generation parameters with results.

Consistent scaling is the default. With `legacy_scaling=TRUE` and
`increase_noise=FALSE`, component targets are scaled by the mixture maximum
while the input mixture remains unscaled. This recreates the training-input
scaling used for the bundled pretrained models. With amplified noise, the
input and targets remain consistently scaled. Zero mixtures are redrawn;
very short degenerate Lorentzian bands use a flat unit band.

Computation is CPU based. Prediction processes each spectrum individually;
`batch_size` is validated but does not enable parallel inference. Large
training batches materialize large convolution patches. Start with small
batches and short runs, then measure memory and elapsed time for your data.
No measured throughput or full training duration is promised.

# Example data and regression checks

```{r bundled-data}
example_path <- system.file("extdata", "synthetic_spectra.csv", package="RADAR")
example_spectra <- RADAR::read(example_path)
example_truth <- load_dataset(system.file("extdata", "synthetic_spectra_truth.rds",
                                         package="RADAR"))
dim(example_truth$X)
```

The five example spectra have 1,024 points, with an axis from 400 to 1,800
inverse centimetres. CSV intensities equal `4000 * example_truth$X + 600`.
Compare predictions with targets on the same intensity scale:

```{r bundled-evaluation}
example_prediction <- RADAR::decompose(example_truth$X, model="standard",
                                       normalize=FALSE)
evaluate_components(example_truth, example_prediction)$peaks
```

The package contains fixed numerical regression fixtures. Tests also cover
finite-difference gradients, decreasing training loss, RDS model round trips,
normalization, maps, file round trips, array order and integer boundaries.
Vendor-file fixtures are synthetic; unusual instrument variants need checking.

# Troubleshooting and practical guidance

| Symptom | Action |
|---|---|
| Missing optional package | Install the dependency reported by `formats()`. |
| Wrong text orientation or axis | Specify `layout`, `delimiter`, `decimal` or `wavenumbers` explicitly. |
| Ambiguous container | Specify the array key, sheet or SQL query. |
| Model file rejected | Use a saved native RADAR `.rds` model and check the requested architecture. |
| Missing map dimensions | Supply `map_shape` and positions where available. |
| Narrow peaks lost | Check how many spectral samples span a band; consider resampling or fine-tuning. |
| Broad peaks mistaken for background | Inspect the baseline and compare representative reference spectra. |
| Strong spikes dominate normalization | Inspect the raw spectrum and decomposition; choose preprocessing for the measurement. |
| Large reconstruction residual | The ensemble predicts four components independently. Inspect residuals before downstream analysis. |
| Out-of-memory training | Reduce batch size, spectral length or network size. |
| Slow inference | Time a small representative sample and process large collections in chunks. |
| Archive writing fails | Ensure a system zip utility is available for NPZ output, or use RDS. |
| Vignette fails to build | Install knitr, rmarkdown and Pandoc; use the prebuilt HTML when reading only. |

Networks are trained on synthetic shapes. Accuracy depends on sampling, band
widths, baseline structure and noise. Retain the measured axis and units and
inspect representative results. A nonnegative predicted peak does not itself
establish a chemical assignment or detection limit.

# Authors, license and citation

Joel Sjöberg contributed the scientific algorithms, network architectures and
pretrained weights. Bogdan Oancea developed the RADAR R package. The package
is distributed under the BSD 3-Clause license, with copyright notices and
conditions in `LICENSE`.

The scientific method is described by Sjöberg, Siminea, Păun, Lita, Larion and
Petre (2025), *RADAR: Raman Spectral Analysis Using Deep Learning for Artifact
Removal*, Advanced Optical Materials, 2500736, DOI: 10.1002/adom.202500736.
Use `citation("RADAR")` for the formatted reference.

# Release 0.1.0

This release includes both pretrained architectures, native R training and
differentiation, synthetic generation, evaluation, spectral file adapters,
map operations, an Rscript interface and the complete guide.
